utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you. Good morning, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the usher could show you a piece of paper, please. Can you confirm that this is your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In the course of this examination, everybody in the courtroom will be referring to you as P-128 or as Witness or as sir, so please do not disclose your identity. And if you see your name or your initials on one of these documents you are shown, you know, please don't read it out. We'll go into private session for that. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, just briefly in terms of your background, can you tell us your nationality, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where are you currently living?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Srebrenik, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you in all briefness describe to the Judges your educational background.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: I completed high school and I'm a mechanical technician. And I completed it in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And currently, what's your current position? What job are you doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: I'm working as a foreman at a petrol station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, in Titovo Uzice and Kraljevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us the year.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: I went to the army in December 1989 and I returned in December 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have a specialisation when you served in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in signal communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us why you chose, if you were able to choose, signals communications.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Because I became a radio amateur very early on. I passed the C-class exam when I was 12 years old in my radio club.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now I would like to focus on the war period. Now, what did you do in 1992 from April on, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: From the month of April 1992, together with some -- together with my colleagues, radio amateurs, we joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: We worked at interceptors -- as radio interceptors.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us the location from which you conducted these activities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Lipik, Majevica, Mountain Majevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, was there a time you were given a new assignment and moved to a different location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes. We were at Lipik for a year and a half, and then we moved to Okresanica, also on Mount Majevica, in the fall of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in Okresanica, were you part of a unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes. We belonged to a unit of the 2nd Corps command from Tuzla. It was called electronic surveillance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, for how long did you stay on Mount Okresanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: I spent -- I was at Okresanica until after the signing of the Dayton Peace Agreement. I was demobilised in January 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the Judges have heard a lot of evidence about the way business was conducted at Okresanica and we don't need to go into details. But can you tell us in one or two sentences what you were doing on Mount Okresanica, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: We were recording conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: When I was working in my shift -- do you mean specifically the way in which we did it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm basically interested in how you recorded it, whether you transcribed it to any form of paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: First of all, the devices scan the channels. When we heard a conversation we would stop; we would turn on the UHER recorders; we would note down the date, the time, and the frequency on a piece of paper, the participants, if we knew who they were, and also the counter number on the UHER. After that, we transferred that to paper, and sent it on to encryption.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What kind of paper was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: They were usually notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: All right. Now I would like to go with you through seven or eight documents. And we would start with the first notebook, that's Prosecution Exhibit 345.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Your Honours, the witness will first talk about an intercept which you find in your first binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Waespi, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but we have a problem with the LiveNote. It's not scrolling. We'll get the technicians to have a look at it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Waespi, would you please try it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Yeah, I don't see anything happening on the screen, unfortunately. Now it seems to move, but it stopped again, so we just wait until it's resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi, can you try it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'll try to move on, because it seems to be working.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, you just explained how you were conducting your business on Mount Okresanica and I believe you said, while the transcript wasn't really picking your voice up, that you were listening to the radios, that you were screening the frequencies, that you were putting it down on pieces of paper, eventually on notebooks, and that you also had the computer which would encrypt these intercepts and send it on. Is that a fair summary of what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I would like to show you a number of these notebooks, and we would start with Prosecution Exhibit 345. If that could be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Your Honours, as I said, it's the first binder. It's tab 14th July. He will talk about Exhibit Number 229. And he will look at the Exhibit 229/D, that's a copy of what he's looking at in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Please, Witness, could you look at a page and it's an eight-number page, but it's sufficient if you look, concentrate on the four last digits, that's 7807 and the next page is 7808. And if you could tell us whether you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And whose handwriting is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, looking at the -- what appears to be a conversation from the left page almost at the top, it starts with a frequency, "frekvencija" in your language. Now, can you tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: This is a transcript of a conversation from the radio relay device. There is the frequency there, the channel, and the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you also see a time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's a time you would put down as you had told us earlier, as soon as you would listen to the conversation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I don't see a date of this intercept. Are you able by looking at your notebook to determine what date, what day, this conversation was intercepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Just one moment, please. The 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how were you able to determine that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: On page 7798.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier that you would also write down the participants. Now, who are the participants in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Zivanovic and Major Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, it doesn't say in the conversation itself that Zivanovic was talking. How were you able to determine that Zivanovic was indeed one of the participants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Because Zivanovic was always recognisable and probably he introduced himself at the beginning of the conversation, but the actual beginning was not recorded. But it was always possible to recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'll ask you about the second participant, Major Jokic. How were you able to determine that it was him talking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: At the very beginning, Zivanovic says his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you also wrote down that he was the duty officer, Palma duty officer. How were you able to determine that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Because very frequently they worked through switchboards, so they would very often say, "Give me the Palma duty officer," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, I would like you to look at the second page of this intercept, that's 7808, and there is a comment at the end. It starts with: "General Zivanovic." Now, can you read out this comment, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: General Zivanovic spoke with distorted voice and was quite unintelligible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, apparently you were able to figure out what he was talking. Can you explain us then what you mean by quite intelligible -- unintelligible, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Always when General Zivanovic spoke, either his telephone was not working properly or he spoke too loudly. So then this would change the modulation of his voice. But with the assistance of my colleagues, I managed to transcribe what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, if you could look at the next exhibit, this is Exhibit P229/D, I believe. And I understand that he has been given the copy already. Can you confirm that this is a true and accurate copy of the original notebook.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, if you could be shown Prosecution Exhibit Number 229/C, please. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the typed or retyped transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And lastly, does this document have a date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes. The 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. If these documents could be returned, and we would go to the second notebook. The second notebook would be Prosecution Exhibit 323.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And for Your Honours that's, again, in the first binder, conversation under tab 14th July, Exhibit Number 230.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you again could have a look at it. And I'm specifically interested in the pages, again last four digits 9704, and the next page which is 9705. The question again is: Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And whose handwriting is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, if we can go -- have a brief look at this conversation. Can you tell us the time it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: At 2048 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, are you able again to determine the date this conversation was recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if Exhibit 230/E could be prepared as well. If it's impossible for you to do that, then you might as well just tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: This is either the 13th or the 14th of July, because the 12th of July is on page 9683.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could have a look at Prosecution Exhibit 230/E.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And again, the same question: Do you recognise this document? This has the same format we have been talking about in the course of the previous document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you see a date on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: I see a date, the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And again, the Exhibit P230/B, is that an accurate copy of the original which you have seen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. If we could move on to the third exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And for your information, Your Honours, it will be eight documents. The next notebook is Exhibit 345. And Your Honours, this is now the second binder, tab 16 July. And that's Exhibit 246.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, if you could have a look at the two pages 7820 and 7821 and tell us whether you recognise the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It's -- I'll tell you the whole range 01077820.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: It's not that notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could have a look. It should be Exhibit 345.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. It's the same notebook he has seen already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that's Prosecution Exhibit 345, again. If you could have a look at the last four digits, 7820.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: I recognise it. It's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, who are the participants to this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Could you just give me the time of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It's 0706, 7.00 and 6 minutes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: The participant is Vinko Pandurevic. The other participant is unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, again we don't see Mr. Pandurevic mentioned at any account during the conversation. Can you tell us again how you were able to figure out that it's Pandurevic talking.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: He probably introduced himself at the beginning of the conversation or it was done judging by his voice, because the beginning was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember how many times you would have listened to his voice during the whole time you were on Mount Okresanica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like you to go down to the middle of the conversation when X says: "Dobro Sefe." Can you read out the whole sentence there, please. In English that would be: "All right, boss." Continue, and so on. Can you read out that line for us, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: "All right, boss. Go on pounding them," and then under a question mark, "and killing them." That is how we would mark a word or several words that we could not understand exactly. But when there is a question mark, it means that this is what we assume the person had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Can you tell us the date again of this intercept, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: The 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And again, just for continuation purposes, Exhibit Number 246/D, is that a copy of that notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could move on, sir, to next exhibit. That's 337. And now this time it's in the notebook 97.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, this can be found under tab 17th July, and it would be Exhibit 266.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could have a look at the page 1282, please. And I'm interested in the top conversation on that page, conversation timed at 1200 hours. Again, my question: Is it your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, it's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And could you tell us again the date it was taken, recorded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: The 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And could you check again whether Exhibit 266/E is an accurate copy of the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you could be shown Exhibit 266/C. And the relevant parts would be on the second page, the last conversation. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we could move on to the next document, that's the fifth document we are dealing with today. This is again Prosecution Exhibit 345. I believe the notebook number was 232.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Your Honours, again second binder, tab 17 July, Exhibit Number 268.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If, sir, you could turn to page 7837 and 38. Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: I recognise the handwriting; it is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us which date it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: I think it's the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If you could compare, again, the copy you have, marked as 268/D, with your original.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you could be shown Exhibit 268/G. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, that could be returned, please. The next exhibit -- in fact, the next two conversations originate from the same notebook, so we can deal with them together. It's Prosecution Exhibit 333, which is notebook number 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's 17th July, and it will be Exhibit 270 and 271.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sir, if you could have a look at both 0639 and 0640. Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, it's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us the date for both conversations, please. One is timed 1244 and the other one timed 1249, according to your handwriting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If you could compare again the two copies of Exhibit 270/B and 271/B with your original.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last part in relation to these two exhibits, if you could be shown 270/E and 271/E, please. And in relation to 270/E, you would need to go to the second page where you find the time 1244. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in relation to P271, the conversation starts at the bottom of the second page, intercept 1249, and goes over to the last page. Do you recognise this document as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could go to the last exhibit this witness is dealing with. This is Prosecution Exhibit 339. That equals notebook number 99. And, Your Honours, that's 18th July, again second binder, and it's Exhibit 287.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could move to page 1480 and 1481. Can you tell us the date of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not understand the witness. Could the answer please be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sir, if you could repeat, please, what you just said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: The 18th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you could compare the copy to the original, and the copy being Exhibit 287/B.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, that's the copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you could be shown the last document, that would be 287/E.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's again a document which was typed, perhaps we can mention it again. Typed by whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Alic Adil.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how quickly after you had given him your notebook would he type up the conversation into the computer. Can you tell us now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Well, very quickly. Five minutes at the most, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my last question to you is the following: We have now seen all these different intercepted conversations which you have transcribed into the notebooks. How accurate and faithful were these transcriptions in relation to the audio, what you could hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Well, most often it is close to 100 per cent, but I will say that the bare minimum, the bare minimum is 90 per cent. But when you listen to all of that you will see that it is almost 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to put a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would kindly ask for us to move into private session because I have a few questions related to his CV and then we will take the other questions in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Listening to all of these witnesses in the past few days, we can have the impression that in this electronic surveillance platoon mostly used soldiers who had experience as ham radio operators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that for this very sensitive work, you did need experience as an amateur radio operator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's try to be more specific. A radio amateur is always more prepared, has more experience, and has better training than any soldier, regular soldier, who is not trained in this field. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, usually it is. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers in your platoon at Okresanica who did not have any ham radio operator experience?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, there were. But the radio amateurs were the ones who started out this whole work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And would you agree that compared to you, these other soldiers were less qualified for this work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes. They were less qualified, but they very quickly managed to learn all about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to move specifically to questions relating to exhibits and questions that the Prosecutor put to you. Could we please ask the usher to give you the notebook P345, and that would be ERN number 01077807. This is an exhibit that you looked at a little bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 01077807. This is a conversation that you had in front of you just a little bit earlier. Is that it there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I apologise, I have to take it a little bit more slowly because of the interpreters, because we are speaking the same language. In answer to a question by the Prosecutor, you said that you didn't know the voice of duty officer Jokic from before and that you noted down that name because General Zivanovic called him by that name in the conversation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Looking at what you wrote down in the notebooks, I didn't notice that there was any other occasion there where you encountered the name Jokic in other intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would we -- can we agree that you did not recognise the voice of the man who introduced himself -- who was introduced as Jokic, but that you did recognise when you heard the voice of General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree, because at that time we were able to recognise people by their voices. These were quite clear conversations, so there was no problem there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I agree. You recognised the voice from before, so you knew General Zivanovic's voice from before and you recognised it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes. It was always recognisable precisely because of the telephone that he used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the voice with the name Jokic is not a voice that you recognised before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: At that time I'm sure I did, but now I wouldn't be able to do it for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: According to your military training and education that you received in the barracks in Kraljevo, do you know that there are several duty officers in the barracks at any given time, the barracks duty officer, the staff command duty officer, the operative duty officer, and also in combat circumstances the duty officer at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Today, responding to a question by the Prosecutor, you said that you wrote duty officer at Palma. If you can look at that, precisely because at the beginning of the conversation this was a person who was requested, the Palma duty officer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you cannot say whether this is the barracks duty officer, the staff command duty officer, the operations officer, the forward command post officer just based on that title. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like you to look at this conversation. If you can just read it quickly, just skim it, and then I will just ask you to answer one question for me about the content of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So I can ask my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is anything mentioned in connection with prisoners anywhere in this conversation? Is the word "prisoners" mentioned anywhere in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: The word "prisoners" is not mentioned anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to clarify another part of it and then we will finish with this conversation. You said that it is true that you did not note down an intercepted conversation anywhere else where Jokic is one of the participants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: I'm -- it's not clear to me, the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In answer to my question a little bit earlier whether you transcribed an intercepted conversation anywhere where the participant is officer Jokic, you said that you did not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that is so, then this answer is not a little bit clear to me that -- when you said it is possible that at that time I did recognise the voice of the person Jokic, because you didn't hear it earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: At that time we recognised the majority of the participants by their voices, because we were always listening, constantly listening to the same people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I understand that. And that is precisely why I know that you said that and I know as a rule whose voices you said you knew from before. You said you recognised several officers of the VRS, and they are Krstic, the voice of Mladic, the voice of Zivanovic, Obrenovic, and Popovic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the voices that I could recall at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I assume that you remembered them better at that time than you do today, because this interview with you was conducted four years ago. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would I be right if I said that you did not recall recognising the voice belonging to a person called Jokic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe he answered the question before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think this is at least the third time for you to ask the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. Everything is all right then. We will continue. Could we again look at an exhibit we saw earlier. This is a notebook P323, and this was also shown to the witness a little bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 00779705.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 705 are the last three digits. Thank you. I just wanted to clarify the following: You said that as a rule because of a lot of concentration, you worked for two or three hours and then you were replaced, a new shift came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Two to three hours of active work when there was a lot of traffic. But shifts could also be longer when the traffic was not so intense.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But as a rule, you would work intensely for two to three hours without interruption?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Well, a shift would generally last for four hours, unless there was a lot of traffic, in which case you could always ask for the replacement shift to begin to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was your platoon commander also in the shifts at that time or did he have other duties or other tasks at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: He had different tasks, and occasionally, only occasionally, he himself would also work at the work stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So I just wanted you to help me to clarify something. Look at the pages that you have in front of you, 9705.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And could you tell me, could I be right if I said on the first third of that page, the conversation that you recorded and transcribed ends, one that you certified with your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific. What are you specifically interested in?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me repeat it. The first third of the page contains the end of that conversation and your signature. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that this conversation from the page before was intercepted at 2048 hours. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next conversation was intercepted at 2102 hours, so 14 minutes later. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, that is probably so. But that is not my conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us whose conversation it is. You don't have to tell us the name of the person, just their title.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Perhaps then I could have told you, but after so long, I no longer recognise the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that on the next page, 00779707, the next intercepted conversation is at 2218 hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So this is one hour and 16 minutes later. And would you agree with me that this is a different handwriting than the one of the previous intercepted conversations, so that these are two different handwritings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Probably it is, but I don't see how that has anything to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since we're going to be mentioning a name, I would just like to move to private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I gave you time to look through the notebook and to try during the break at least to see whether you ever noted down these intercepted conversations in which, like you mentioned a little bit earlier, you heard the person called Jokic, would that help you, because we didn't find such conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether that would help me, but I did hear that name before, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you heard it, then I assume you should have written it down in the notebook. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no more questions, Your Honours. In view of the fact that it would take a lot of time for the witness to go through the notebooks to see that there are no messages with his handwriting which record the name of Jokic. So thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Witness, I would like you to clarify your statement that in 1995 you have been able to recognise the voice of Major Jokic, but now you couldn't recognise it. What do you mean, that you did forget his voice or something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-128
utterances.text: It's normal after so many years to forget these things, but we did listen to these voices very often at that time, so it was very easy to recognise them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, are there any questions out of Judge's question? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, at this stage, are there any documents to tender? Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this point I would only like to tender Prosecution Exhibit 351, that's the pseudonym sheet. But after the break perhaps we would like to tender -- my colleague Ms. Issa will do that, the two binders, because we are now at the end of these intercept witnesses, and I think that's the best moment to go into that exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Are there any objections to the document P351? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. This document is admitted into the evidence. Well, as I instructed both parties that this is the last witness in that group, so I hope after this witness that both parties, if they will have some documents to tender, especially those intercept documents, please send us a list. We only want that list. Then we will give the parties a week to respond to those lists. So next Monday I hope we could receive any objections or responses concerning those intercepts. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. We all wish you a good journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the room. Before we have the recess, Mr. Waespi, we have another witness waiting this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This will be Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll continue our proceedings with the next witness. And I've noticed that -- yes, Mr. Blagojevic. THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave I would like to say a few sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may. THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] In mid-September this year, here in this courtroom I submitted a request. I asked to have a meeting with Mr. Sokran [phoen], independent counsel. This was not done, although my request was not refused then or later. The next thing I wish to say is the following: I have to say yet again that I have none, I underline none, no legal protection or legal representation before this Tribunal. Therefore, I am very concerned over the next stage of the proceedings. I can say to you that it has come to my knowledge that a person was dismissed, or rather, sacked, namely the last member of the Defence team, let's call it the Defence team, who was involved as my choice. And now all of this is being done until now and now, all of this is being done without any influence coming from me or without any involvement of mine. I'm asking you, Your Honours, how can this happen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Blagojevic, I would like to draw your attention to a decision rendered by the Appeals Chamber concerning of the substantive issue as for your application to change your Defence team, which was rendered on the 7th November, 2003. I hope this decision will be translated into the language you understand as soon as possible. So if you have some difficulties concerning with this decision, please do not hesitate to let this Bench know. Up to now we haven't received any filings from your part, so actually we don't know what your request is. My suggestion is that if you have any requests, you may raise it to the registrar. And this Bench will see what we can do in this respect. THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if this pertains to the first sentence I uttered, or rather, the request that I submitted here before you orally, in all fairness, then I can submit that request to the registrar, that is no problem for me. But since I did not receive a full decision, and this previous decision of the Appeals Chamber, I didn't receive that either, and now you're telling me this decision was passed on the 7th of November, 2003, then I'm going to have a look at it and I'll see what stems from that. I cannot say anything more specific at this stage, because I am not aware of the contents fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We will bear your request in mind, but we will continue the proceedings this morning. You may sit down, please. THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I've noticed that a representative of the U.S. Government is present in this courtroom. For the sake of the record, would you please identify yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My name is David Kay and I'm the deputy legal counsellor at the American Embassy here in The Hague. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In accordance with our ruling rendered last week, you are allowed to be present in these proceedings and submit any interventions which you believe will infringe upon the interests of your government. Could we have the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Would you please make the solemn declaration, please. 1

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours and good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you please state your name?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: My name is Richard Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: I am a U.S. Citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you a member of the United States army for many years?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: That is correct. I was a member of the United States army from August 1981 to September 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From 1981 to 1983, you were an enlisted man in the army. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: From 1981 to 1987, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And from 1983 to 1988 you were a non-commissioned officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And from 1988 until the time you retired, you were a warrant officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you retire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: I retired 30th September, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then just briefly, you worked for the United Nations for a short time and then you have now gone on and will expect a job in the United States government in January?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, you've spent most of your time in the army as a warrant officer, what is a warrant officer as opposed to a regular officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: A warrant officer is an officer who is prepped to deal with specialised technical issues, intelligence -- the technical issue of intelligence. There are warrant officers in the logistics field. There are warrant officers in aviation. What that means is that that career pattern is tracked to allow for the warrant officer to spend his entire military career working within the confines of his technical expertise. In the sense of other officers, regular officers, they will be expected as part of their normal career pattern to do things outside of the normal career focus, such as teaching ROTC classes for several years, they will be expected to do recruiting duty, they will be expected to do other types of normal, out-of-track service. So as a warrant officer, our career track is specifically designed to keep us focused on our narrow career fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As an army warrant officer, you have lots of abbreviations. Some of them we're not familiar with. ROTC?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: ROTC is Reserve Officers Training Corps. That is the programme where active military officers are instructors at universities and colleges teaching classes for college students who will one day become army officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was your specialty as a warrant officer in your career?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: My specialty, I was referred to as an all-source intelligence technician. So my specialty revolved around information and intelligence with respect to combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe in a little more detail what this job entailed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: As an all-source intelligence technician, what the job normally entails and what it did entail in my case, was the ability to take intelligence or information from a variety of sources, that would include human intelligence, it would include signals intelligence, open source-based intelligence, combat information. Essentially to take in all of this information in order to analyse it, synthesise it, and then be able to take that information and present it back to the commander who I'm supporting and allow that commander to have the best possible picture of the battle operating environment that he's in or the strategic picture that he's facing. Again, that allows the commander to make the most informed decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you briefly go through with us what kind of experience and training and schooling you had for that job. Just briefly, if you could.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: As a -- in the military, my first course was, of course, in 1981, which was the basic military intelligence course as an enlisted person. In 1986, I believe it would be -- 1985 I think. It was the non-commissioned officers course for intelligence analysis. In 1988, when I became a warrant officer, it was the warrant officer technical certification course. Then following that it was the warrant officer advanced technical certification course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about a college degree? Did you get a college degree anywhere in there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: I have a bachelor's degree from the University of Maryland, European division, in political science.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you please define and describe the three subject areas of military analysis.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Within the framework of military analysis, with the focus on land warfare, there are three general areas. What we call the strategic form of analysis, operational analysis, and tactical analysis. Strategic analysis, as the name implies, is a form of analysis that has to do with a larger body of nations, their political military structure, their military industrial structure and how that supports the military and political objectives. The operational level corresponds to the operational level of war where the analyst looks at and studies the aspects of corps and army operations, those types of longer-term operations and how armies and corps and division interrelate. And at the tactical level what we're looking at is the more micro focus on the battle field. We're looking at from the division to the brigade to the battalion. Those types of -- forms of intelligence analysis that are directly relevant to combat commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Have you been assigned to a combat theatre in your career?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could get the CV of Mr. Butler which I believe is Exhibit 355. And if we could just place that on the ELMO on page 2.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: This starts on -- page 1 actually is my assignment history.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I don't want to go in detail of that, but these -- this brief outline beginning with analysis of the former Warsaw Pact, military forces, and going down to 1992 to 1997 --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Going chronologically from April 1997, of course, to present will be working in support of this institution. August 1992 to March 1997, my focus was dealing with issues pertaining to southwest Asia. And it was during that time when I was dealing with southwest Asia that I had my combat experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And does the rest of the CV reflect your other experiences?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It reflects my time in Europe studying the Warsaw Pact as it was back then. It reflects time in the United States doing time with tactical-based units and some of the more strategic assignments that I've had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And when did you begin work for the United Nations Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: I began working for the Office of the Prosecutor in April 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you still an active army warrant officer at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe your arrangement between the Office of the Prosecutor and the United States, if any?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: During that period of time, when the secondment programme still existed through the United Nations, I as well as a number of other individuals were seconded by the United States government in support of the ICTY as the institution, and in my particular case in support of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for most of your time working here, you have concentrated on the Srebrenica investigation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. I started working directly supporting the Srebrenica investigation in June of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the tasks and objectives of your assignments related to that investigation.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: As the military analyst assigned to that investigation team, what I was asked to do was essentially develop the military overlay for the various crime scenes that were under investigation. So that was in respect doing my research and analysis, determining what the relevant military units were in and around that area, what the relevant police units were, what the command and control interrelationships were, and as that developed, then the next piece of analysis began looking for pieces of information that may or may not tie specific units or specific individuals to the crime scenes as they were identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did that include studying the basic military doctrine that may have been in effect at the time in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That was the first step.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a minor point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know we're still in the background, but I would appreciate it if we can get the testimony from the witness as opposed to the leading nature of that question, Your Honour. I know we want to speed things up, but at some point I just -- I don't want to be jumping up and down and objecting to leading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, as you said we are still on the fields of the background issues. In this area, the leading questions are allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the work that you've just very briefly described for the OTP, which of the three areas of analysis did it involve: Strategic, operational, or tactical or some combination thereof?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: In this particular case with Srebrenica, it involved all three. The first step, of course, the part of the strategic analysis was understanding how the army of the Republika Srpska or the VRS, was organised and how it operated within the framework of the political leadership of the VRS. How it was supported, how it was organised, how it was resourced. It dealt with the operational level, because the next step was basically, once we understood that, how it operated and regulated itself in a military or a combat environment. That was where the understanding of the rules and the regulations of the former JNA and how they applied to the VRS worked in, as well as the interrelationship between the army level, which in this case would be the VRS Main Staff, and the corps level, in this case the Drina Corps, and how it also related to the police who were also part of the armed forces. Then at the final level, the tactical level, the ability to understand at the brigade and battalion level how those units acted, how they were commanded, and how that interrelated with the corps level. So with respect to the Srebrenica operation, I had to draw on my background in all three areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did your -- the results of your study and analysis take the form of any reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: With respect to my preparations for the trial of General Krstic, I produced two reports. I produced a corps command responsibility report, which delineated the responsibilities of a VRS corps commander in July of 1995. And I also did a report I call the Srebrenica military narrative, which is the actual fact basis which discusses the linkage between the Drina Corps, General Krstic, and those crimes that were investigated on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Have you made similar reports for this trial?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, how do they -- just very briefly, relate to the Krstic reports? Are they completely new or what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, sir, they are structured very similar. The report that I did in this particular case is called "the VRS Brigade Command Report". And in this instance what I have done is taken much of the same information and tailored it to the roles and responsibilities of a VRS brigade commander during the period in question. As for the Srebrenica military narrative, building on my original product, what I've done is I've revised that, again tailoring it in some respects to the brigade level as well as using it as an opportunity to add a lot of new information that has come into possession of the OTP over the intervening years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And for the command report, can you give us not a complete but a general idea of the kinds of materials you relied on in writing that report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: For the most part, the foundation is set on a series of former JNA, Yugoslav national army, rules and regulations, which in effect regulate how combat operations are conducted and how the associated support functions are conducted. One of the very first things that I had to do as part of the analytical process, in order to understand how the army worked was to determine their operating rules and regulations. In this particular case with the VRS, for the most part, not totally, but for the most part, they fully adopted the rules and regulations of the JNA. And given the fact that most of the people who were involved in senior leadership positions were formerly from the JNA, that obviously made a certain amount of sense. Other things that I used were instructions, documents, and orders that the VRS itself had produced, which the Office of the Prosecutor had acquired through a series of seizures or had come in through a number of other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how thorough or how complete were the various manuals and instructions that you, in this investigation, assembled over the years?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: I think it is pretty thorough. Obviously we are missing some manuals that we would like to have that we just have not been able to acquire. Certainly in the form of documents, there are missing documents that we would like to acquire, but I think that we have enough of a broad scope of material to be able to say that we have a relatively complete picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, for example, did you recently get some new regulations in an area of concern for this trial?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Specifically within the last few days the Defence has turned over the JNA manuals on engineering regulations which were not in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor. So those are the type of documents that we continue to look for as part of building the overall completeness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But not having those regulations, does that damage your ability to understand the position of engineering officers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Not particularly, because we're able to reconstruct a lot of that same material from the 1984 brigade regulations and other various documents that we do have. So in many cases, it's just a confirmation that the VRS was still using the procedures envisioned by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, the command report is Prosecution's number 357.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, for the narrative report for this trial, can you describe the kinds of materials, and I know we're going to be going at length into specific materials, but can you just give the Chamber an idea of the kinds of materials you were reviewing and analysing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: With respect to the narrative report, probably the most significant series of documents were those documents that were seized by the Office of the Prosecutor in 1998 from what was formerly the Zvornik Infantry Brigade and the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. Those documents formed the foundation for the knowledge of how those two specific organisations functioned during the war and how they functioned specifically in July 1995. Since then there are other documents that have also come in that also play important parts. For example, the Office of the Prosecutor has seized documents from CSB Zvornik and from the RS MUP headquarters which overlay and give more detail as to the relationship between the army and the MUP. And of course that's a key component of the events of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what CSB Zvornik means.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: CSB is the centre for security. I mean, that's their regional police station or regional security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And since the completion of your narrative for this trial, have new documents come in that were not cited in your narrative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: In that respect, there are two new categories of documents that we've obtained that are not in that narrative. The first -- and when I say "narrative," I would also add I did publish an addendum to chapter 8 which does reflect some of the new material. But with this respect, material that's not is would be material that we received from the -- when the OTP did a -- conducted a search of the RS-RDB headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: The RS-RDB is the Republika Srpska state security. We acquired some of their documents when we searched the headquarters of the RS Ministry of the Interior. Those provide a background of what the state leadership and the intelligence service had access to with forms of information during July 1995. And also documents that were provided by Mr. Obrenovic were also not incorporated into the narrative at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, since you and the witness are speaking the same language, just make a pause. And witness, I understand that you are eager to give your evidence. So whatever you say has to be in the transcript. So please say it slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you use open-source material in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: We did use open-source material. Much of that what we call open-source material would in fact be military magazines published by the Republika Srpska, several news clippings from non-Bosnian newspapers for issues pertaining to notice. But for the most part we relied on the military documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you rely on any investigative materials such as crime scene information, witness interviews?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: I have talked about some of the issues with witness interviews only in the part or only in the sense of trying to establish the broader context of where the military documents fit into a story that a witness would say. So where I used witness statements or where I used, for example, testimony out of the Krstic case is only to create the context of what the witness has already said or testified on and where the military documents may or may not relate to that. I don't use witness statements or testimony that's been heard in court as a fundamental component of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just, for example, in the Krstic trial, Muslim witnesses identified by name several Serbs that were present in Potocari. Did you -- how did you analyse the names of the Serbs that were provided in the testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: In that instance, what I would do is taking that witness's testimony, I would then verify or cross-index whether or not those names of individuals showed up on military document listings showing that they're members of a certain unit. So that would be a good example of where I would take a witness testimony and use it to set the foundations, so to speak, for why these military documents are now relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at times in the investigation did you sit in on any interviews of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: I sat in during the investigation in numerous interviews, and on those interviews where I was not able to go because of other commitments, I read the interviews after they were finished. So I have access to all of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why were you actually present during interviews of various people?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, certainly during the early days of the investigation and the initial interviews that we started conducting in 1998, as the military analyst, logically I was the person who had the broadest background as to the military context of the individual and the questions that would be asked. Most of these interviews were, in fact, of VRS military officers. So it was pretty much, you know, a logical conclusion that I would be a person in there to be able to assist investigators and the lawyers who were present as a component of preparing for and in the interview to determine not how accurate the individual is speaking, but to ensure that on follow-on questions, we can get complete answers with respect to military issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. As part of your narrative and as a part of your analysis, did you review Bosnian Muslim army and Bosnian MUP intercepts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in reviewing them, did you make any judgement about them regarding their value to your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: As we obtained the initial products from the intercepts in 1998 and I believe I testified to this extent in the Krstic trial, I was, of course, very skeptical of this product. And as a component of my analysis, once we had these indexed and once they were translated in bulk, which means I could look at the entire month and the entire periods in context, the first thing I would do in looking at these intercepts is to try and cross-index them to events we know occurred on the ground or documents we know occurred -- or documents we have where we can say reasonably that the Bosnian Muslim army would never have access to this information. I also made myself aware of the collection environment that the Bosnian Muslims were collecting against and their tactics and procedures in doing that. So as I worked with this body of information over a two-year period prior to the Krstic case and even today, I've gained a great deal of confidence in this material that it, in fact, represents the actual context of many of the things that were happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. For the record, the narrative is P358, and the addendum to it is P359. Now, you make, as we all know, many citations to many sources in your narrative and your command report. One in particular was the United Nations report to the General Assembly on Srebrenica. What did you rely on that report for?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, as I've indicated in the introduction to my Srebrenica military narrative, the goal of the narrative is rather focused to the issues of the military, the VRS, the Drina Corps, and its interrelation with the crime scenes. It is not a report which is designed to be an all-encompassing historical perspective of the war in the Drina Valley or the Podrinje region from 1992 to 1995. I rely on that report because that report does offer a very broad contextual basis of the military and political events that are occurring from 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that report, Your Honour, has been specially marked as P360, the UN report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Butler, I want you to take us through some of the key elements of your command report with some help from some -- we'll start off with some charts that I know you have made. And the first area I'd like you just to provide us a brief outline on is the structure of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska. And I think that is best shown by an exhibit that you've developed, P361, a chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It may be simpler for Mr. Butler just to place his copies on the ELMO. They are marked with the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Butler, first of all, could you just give us a brief outline of the structure of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Under RS law, the armed forces are defined as two entities. One, of course, is the army. The other, of course, is the Ministry of the Interior, or MUP. So those are the two branches of the Republika Srpska armed forces. With respect to the army, there are six ground corps which are -- which represent the combat power of the army. And of course those are listed on the chart there. And the corps that's most relevant to this trial will of course be the Drina Corps. Also as part of the army are two other units that are independent, insomuch as they don't answer to a corps, they answer directly to the Main Staff. One of them is the 65th Protection Regiment and the other one is the 10th Sabotage Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe what the 65th Protection Regiment is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: The 65th Protection Regiment is, again, is an organisation that is a holdover from the former JNA protection regiment. It is a unit that is designed to provide security primarily for military district-type headquarters and strategic facilities. During the course of the war, with the VRS, this unit, the 65th Protection Regiment, also played an additional role not only in guarding such facilities, but it also played an important role on the battlefield, because it was one of the best equipped and best trained units in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in particular to the Srebrenica situation, what role -- and very briefly, where was it? What role did it play?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, with respect to the combat formations and manoeuvre formations, they didn't play a role in Srebrenica at all as far as we can determine. However, the unit did have a military police battalion, and that battalion was garrisoned at Nova Kasaba. That battalion does play a role in the events that occurred around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you give us the same brief description of the 10th Sabotage Detachment.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: As described by both Mr. Erdemovic primarily and other accounts, the 10th Sabotage Detachment was utilised during the final assault on the urban area of Srebrenica itself. And later it comes into play as a portion of the unit that was involved with the massacres at the Branjevo Military Farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And generally what kind of unit was the 10th Sabotage Unit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: It was organised specifically to do covert or clandestine sabotage operations against strategic targets against the army of Bosnia. So in this particular case they were specifically trained to operate in small units and sabotage, demolition or strategic intelligence collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And who is the commander in chief of the armed forces in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, the commander in chief of the armed forces, again by their law, would be Dr. Radovan Karadzic, who is the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now let's go into a brief outline of the Main Staff. So we'll go from 361 which is a very rough chart to this more specific chart of P362 of the Main Staff. And can you just start with the top, Mr. Butler, and talk to us about who these people are and how -- just give us a very brief background of what the Main Staff's function was and who -- first of all, what the Main Staff function was. And secondly, who are some of these individuals in the structure and where we should be looking for them in the events in question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, the Main Staff as an organisation was the entity that effectively commanded and controlled the armed forces -- or not the armed forces. To be specific, it controlled the army. The commander of the Main Staff at the time was Lieutenant Colonel General Ratko Mladic. He had a deputy who at the time Lieutenant Colonel Manojlo Milovanovic. He was called the chief of the Main Staff, but he performed the role of the deputy commander. Now, in July of 1995, he is not functioning in his role as deputy commander. One of the things that occurred as a result of the military situation in the northern part of the country, the Main Staff established a forward command post in Banja Luka controlling the activities of the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps. And General Milovanovic was detailed to command that. As a result, that position was filled by General Major Radivoje Miletic who was the chief of operations. This is consistent with the former JNA doctrine which indicates that when the chief of staff is absent, the position is filled by the chief of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just briefly, will we see General Miletic later on in some of the documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: We will see General Miletic in a document identified as the acting chief of the Main Staff on 12 July, 1995. And we will also see intercepts which feature conversations with General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
