utterances.text: Okay. If you could continue along this diagram going from the left to the right, identifying anyone that -- and just give us a brief kind of preview of where we might be seeing them as we go through some of the documents.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: In the combat services of the branch, Colonel Trkulja and Colonel Sladojevic are operations officers. They are here and here. Both of those individuals will be featured in a 17 July Main Staff order being sent to the Zvornik Brigade to conduct an investigation into the events that occurred with respect to the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's -- we'll get into that in a little more detail later. But let's continue on left to right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Looking now at the department of security and intelligence affairs, that is headed, of course, by General Major Zdravko Tolimir. We have documents which now indicate that General Tolimir was at the Drina Corps headquarters in Vlasenica on 12th July. From the intelligence administration, some of the other people we would see would be Colonel Radislav Jankovic who features on 11 July 1995 as one of the individuals, with General Mladic, at the first meeting of the Hotel Bratunac. He also conducts reports on the conduct of the movement of the people from Potocari to Kladanj. And he is also involved with dealing with issues of wounded Bosnian Muslims who were under care and transferred to the Bratunac medical centre. So we will see him through the continuing 11 to 17, 18 July period. Colonel Milovan Stankovic is also an intelligence officer. We will see his presence in Zvornik as part of this investigating commission of officers on 17th July. Lieutenant Colonel -- for the intelligence side, that's pretty much all that we'll see. On the other side, the security administration affairs, one of the first people and one of the prominent players we'll see is Colonel Ljubo Beara, who is the chief of security. We first see him in the area of Bratunac or in that general area in 11.00 on 13 July when he's involved in a conversation concerning prisoners at Nova Kasaba. He is a constant player in the activities through 18 July. Major Pecanac has been identified as a security officer who is primarily concerned with security of General Mladic. We have a document from him dated 12 July 1995 which is an intelligence report which he authored from Bratunac. Lieutenant Colonel Keserovic is a security officer who is charged with oversight of the military police of the Republika Srpska. We will see his presence on the 17th as an officer who's detailed to assume command or control of various units sweeping the terrain in and around Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go over to the department for moral, religion and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel General Milovan Gvero is the assistant commander for moral, religious, and legal affairs of the army. We have visibility on him in the form of a document where he is with General Krstic on the evening of 9th of July at the forward command post. Below him is Lieutenant Colonel Milovan Milutinovic who functions as the public affairs officer for the VRS. We have him in and around the Bratunac area, and some of the video footage that was taken of the Hotel Fontana meetings was in fact by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go now to the other main structure of the armed forces that you mentioned briefly. And that is the -- under the Ministry of the Interior. And we have an exhibit P363. And can you, like you did before, briefly describe to us the structure, first of all, and then give us a briefest of outlines of who these people are and where we might be seeing them.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: At the time in question, Tomislav Kovac is the acting minister of the interior. Subsequent to this he becomes the minister of interior. We see his name featured in the 10 July 1995 order directing that elements of the special police brigade be sent to the Srebrenica battle front. We'll also see Mr. Kovac, his physical presence approximately 14 July in and around the Bratunac and Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next two boxes begin with CJB Zvornik and then special police brigade. Now, the Trial Chamber has heard a fair amount of information on this, but could you just give us the briefest outline of the differences of these two outfits, what their functions are.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, in that time period, the police were organised into two separate entities -- I mean, two significant separate entities. There are smaller ones, obviously. But in this respect, the CSBs, the regional security centres, public security centres, are organised, their primary function is law enforcement within the Republika Srpska. As a component of that primary function and due to shortage of manpower with the VRS in general. The CSBs were directed to have available police officers who could be organised into companies and be sent to battlefield on short notice for short periods of time. Those are what we call the PJP companies. Those are special police companies but they are made up of the municipal police. On the other side, the police also had what they called a special police brigade which was organised for more strategic anti-terrorism operations, things of that nature. They were also organised into detachments of roughly two company or battalion size. And like the PJP counterparts, when required, they were also used in combat operations to make up for manpower. So there are two distinct branches, however, in practice they often worked very closely with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And is this exhibit P363, does it reflect a particular time frame and operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: This particular exhibit reflects my understanding of the police infrastructure and relationships in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I will go over some of the names as we get to them. I don't think we need to go over them right now. All right. Now, as we work our way towards the -- understanding the Drina Corps and where it fits into the structure, can we just take a brief look at Exhibit 364 which -- and tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: If we could scan out just a little bit. Thank you. This is a computer-generated map which I have done based off of VRS maps and documents that we have which lays out the zone of the Drina Corps in July of 1995. Just for reference, this is the Srebrenica safe area. This will be the Zepa safe area. And down here is the Gorazde safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this map roughly to scale?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so what's the distance roughly from the perimeter of the Zepa safe area and the Srebrenica safe area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Generally, while its straight line, 10 to 15 kilometres. Again, nothing in that region is straight line because of the terrain, so you're looking at -- it's going to be a little bit longer route because you have to follow the terrain contours. So it's about 15 to 20 kilometres perimeter-to-perimeter wise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And while we've got them up there, let me just ask you briefly: What was the problem the VRS was facing in July of 1995 when they talk about communication between the two enclaves? We'll go into this entire historical thing a little more deeper. While we see the two enclaves there, can you tell us what was going on.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, with respect to Srebrenica and Zepa, there was, for the most part, an active crossing of troops back and forth, as you will. There was essentially three brigades of the 28th Division in Srebrenica. There was another brigade of that division in Zepa. And there was a constant amount of travel back and forth between the soldiers. Where this became a problem particularly for the VRS is that, particularly for elements of the Bratunac, Skelani and Milici units, is that there used to be frequent ambushes in this area and of course it would be a constant manpower drain in controlling it, and particularly the Skelani unit would take a significant amount of casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just briefly, in the larger picture of the war, how did this affect the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, always going back to the position that one of the significant shortfalls in the VRS was a lack of manpower to -- for the frontage that they held. This particular situation with these safe areas meant that a number of combat formations, particularly units like the Bratunac Brigade, the Milici Brigade, Skelani brigade, the Visegrad Brigade and Rogatica Brigade were tied down in these areas here and their manpower was not available for other areas of the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that the specific intention of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt the gentleman but if we could have a foundational question. Now he's being asked to speculate at this point. If he has a basis or has come across some documents or something that would give us some comfort that he's not speculating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Lay some foundations for us before you ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The question will lead to the foundation, Your Honour. But I can go on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we come to the issue of the chicken first or the egg first. But you may ask some questions to this witness concerning the foundations and later on come to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One of the reasons I asked the question like that is I believe it's part of Mr. Karnavas's case, as it is with ours, that this was a deliberate policy of the Muslim army to tie down VRS troops. It's stated in documents that Mr. Butler's read. So I didn't know I would get an objection, but I know Mr. Karnavas likes to keep me strictly to the way he does, so we can -- that's all we're doing. I'll try to go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just briefly, have you reviewed documents that indicate what the BiH army's policy was towards the military actions in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Certainly as the war progressed the ABiH government recognised the strategic value of having those forces tied around the enclaves as opposed to being used in other more critical fronts of the battlefield. The one advantage that the ABiH did have over the VRS was in numbers. As a result one of the patterns we would see is when the ABiH was launching operations in an area, one of the best examples would be the Sarajevo 1995 offensive by the ABiH. That what the 28th Infantry Division, and it was known in July 1995, was directed to do was to launch offensive operations in order to prevent forces from the Drina Corps and these forces specifically from being used to reinforce battlefields in and around the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's now get off that little diversion and go back to the Drina Corps, back to our structure of the Drina Corps. And I think in order to assist your testimony, let's have P365. And can you tell us -- again, describe to us where the Drina Corps fit in and very briefly how it was organised. And we'll start going through the chart in particular.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, the Drina Corps was organised consistent with the way that former JNA corps were organised. So by using that, it shows the JNA model and this is how that corps was built. This chart reflects my understanding of the key personalities on 13th July, 1995, when General Radislav Krstic assumed command of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So can you just describe briefly how these corps are structured, how their command staffs are structured and what kind of units they have with them.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, in tandem to the Main Staff which was organised having branches for operations, moral, legal, and religious affairs, the security and rear services, the corps organisation and the corps staff is organised along the same manner. You will have a corps commander. You will have a corps chief of staff who functions as the deputy commander in the absence of the commander, or if the commander is not available. You will have as part of the corps staff your operations department, personnel, and intelligence. You will have a security department. You will have a department for moral, religious, and legal affairs. And you will have your department for rear services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what about the actual combat units under the corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: In this context, what the VRS did for the most part was organise their forces under a corps brigade structure. So while the corps staff was the commanding and directing entity of the corps, the actual combat power of the formation was in its brigades. So in this particular case, the Drina Corps had a number of brigades. And in some cases some separate battalions that represented the bulk of its power.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's do like we did before and just very briefly identify the people in the various positions and just where we might be seeing them as we go through the rest of the narrative.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Starting with the top, obviously, with General Major Radislav Krstic. We see him first as the Chief of Staff and then later as the commander of the Drina Corps. He is a principle player in designing the operation to initially reduce Srebrenica to its urban area, and then later take the actual city itself. And of course his troops were involved and he is involved with a lot of the events that occur after the fall of the safe area. The chief of staff position on 13th July is nominally filled by then-Colonel Svetozar Andric, who was the commander of the Birac Infantry Brigade. However, due to the fact that his brigade was involved in combat operations in Zepa at the time, we don't believe that he actually assumed the position of chief of staff of the brigade during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you talk briefly about General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, General Zivanovic was the corps commander until approximately between 1800 and 2000 hours on 13th July, 1995. While General Krstic was responsible for organising the operation and the actual conduct of it at the IKM, General Zivanovic was the corps commander. And certainly by the 10th of July, General Zivanovic was down there overseeing the operation with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's in this brief overview again start with the operations and training section. And just give us the briefest of -- if you recognise any of these individuals as being significant later on down the road.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: In this particular case the first person would be the chief of operations Colonel Obrad Vicic. For the most part he is accompanying General Krstic. He is up at the forward command post, the IKM Pribicevac. And it is his function to direct the actual combat operations and make sure those are fully coordinated. Other officers we will see, Colonel Slavko Ognjenovic and Colonel Predrag Jocic. Their names as Drina Corps officers will show up in intercepts or in actual documents that delineate their position. For example, on 13 July 1995, Colonel Predrag Jocic is the duty officer of the Drina Corps. And on the 13th and 14th he is responsible, as the duty officer, for passing information to the corps commanders and to also subordinate brigades. As the section for reinforcement, Radenko Jovicic. He is visible by virtue of a document, which is signed by him, noting that the change of command between General Zivanovic and General Krstic on the 13th of July. In the intelligence section, Lieutenant Colonel Kosoric is an intelligence officer. He is the chief of intelligence for the Drina Corps. You see him, of course, he goes down with General Krstic and his presence is noted at the Hotel Fontana in a series of meetings. And also as a focal point we'll see him in many documents that are transmitted concerning information derived from prisoner of war interrogations. Major Golic is an intelligence officer. During the period that Colonel Kosoric is in the field, Major Golic is at the Drina Corps headquarters. We will see him author some of the intelligence reports that go to the Bratunac Brigade, that go to the Zvornik Brigade and are sent to the forward command post. One thing that I do want to note before we leave that in the corps staff is you will note that underneath is the name of Colonel Nedjo Blagojevic. As the chief of security or chief of communications within the Drina Corps. I note this because in the context of intercepts and in the context of other documents, I have to take this into account if we have an identification with only a last name, that one of the accused, you know, shares that last name with him and therefore I'm cognizant of that fact when I go into my analysis of who the correspondents of a discussion are. Moving now to the security department. The key player is in this particular case Lieutenant Colonel Vujadin Popovic, who is the chief of security of the Drina Corps. We see his presence in Potocari on -- or we see his presence in the Bratunac area first on the morning of 12 July. And he is a featured player in intercepts and also other documents with respect to the mass executions of Bosnian Muslim men. Colonel Slobodan Cerovic is the chief or he is the assistant commander for moral, legal, and religious affairs and has guidance, but it's translated two different ways. In this particular case we see him, one witness places him in Potocari on the 12th of July. But primarily where we'll see him involved is as a duty officer in the Drina Corps on the 15th and 16th of July where his name comes up in intercepts referring to orders related to the execution of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And how about for the department for rear services?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: I'll just fold this over a bit. A number of these individuals are -- will be associated with the movement of the Bosnian Muslims from Potocari to Kladanj. And their names come up with respect to the resources needed to do that as well as the buses which will ultimately move the Bosnian Muslim men from collection centres in and around Bratunac to the zone of the Zvornik Brigade. First among these is the assistant commander or the chief of rear services, Colonel Lazar Acamovic. We will see references to Lieutenant Colonel Rajko Krsmanovic who is the head of the transportation service of the Drina Corps. We will see his name frequently with respect to buses and other means of transportation. The chief of the technical service, Major Tomislav Basevic, his name is featured in a series of intercepts with respect to 16th July, 1995, where because of the execution operations they need more fuel and Basevic is the head of technical services, represents the approval of authority for this fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you just point out which of the actual brigades we may be hearing about. And again, very -- we're not going detail here, but just mention the ones that we may be hearing of.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: If we can just zoom in a little bit, please. Thank you. The Birac Infantry Brigade, the first unit there, they're involved in combat operations with respect to Srebrenica and Zepa. The Vlasenica Infantry Brigade, their involvement is with respect to having reserve forces available as well as a component of their forces are at the last point of departure from the RS for buses of Muslims being evacuated or moved out of the enclave. So they are the forces that when you hear at Kladanj, at the -- those are the forces of the Vlasenica Brigade. The Zvornik Infantry Brigade as you're aware from the testimony of Colonel Obrenovic, is involved in both the actual military capture of Srebrenica, as well as the criminal events that follow in their zone. The Milici Light Infantry Brigade, there again they have a part in the actual takedown of Srebrenica, although its primarily defensive in nature. Their units are also involved in Zepa. However, forces of the Milici brigade do capture Bosnian Muslim men along the road on 12 and 13 July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And just very briefly for the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, Bratunac, by virtue of their location, they have a part to play in both the actual capture of Srebrenica and they're also involved in the issue with the movement of people out of Potocari and on the Bosnian Muslim men around that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Skelani Separate Battalion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: That unit as far as we can determine has no active role in anything other than operations regarding the takedown of Srebrenica. They are not involved in anything following that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: The Rogatica Brigade is in fact dealing with issues related to Zepa. So in this particular case with Srebrenica, their only involvement is when the focus of the VRS operation shifts from Srebrenica to Zepa, they will become involved. But with respect to any potential criminal activity, there is no known involvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You may need to slow down a bit. Visegrad Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: The Visegrad Brigade is again primarily involved with operations around Zepa. Where we see this involvement with respect to some of the crimes related to Srebrenica is that on 13th and 15th of July, there are references to one unit of the Visegrad brigade, or the 5th Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade as it's also known, being asked for use in a mass execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The next one, the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: The 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade had elements involved in the actual military operation to take down or capture the Srebrenica town. There's no known involvement with them in any of the criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the 5th Engineering Battalion, and can you describe briefly what this is, where they're located.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: The 5th Engineering Battalion is located in the village of Konjevic Polje at the intersection. They represent the corps's engineer unit, primarily bridging assets, earth moving equipment, combat engineer related functions. Of course their garrison being in Konjevic Polje, they are involved in the programme or process where prisoners are being taken. Several of their soldiers are killed or injured as a result of that on 12 and 13 July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And the 5th Mixed Artillery Regiment.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Just as the engineer battalion is where the engineering equipment for the corps is, the 5th Mixed Artillery Regiment is the corps' artillery regiment. In this particular case, most of its assets are deployed in or around the area of Pribicevac and are involved in providing fire support for military forces conducting operations at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The 5th Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: This battalion organisation of military police is generally not seen in and around the Srebrenica area. The best information that we have is that as has happened in many cases in the past with the VRS, the military police unit, because it represents a reserve of manpower that can be used, instead of being used for traditional law enforcement functions is used as a combat formation. The best knowledge that we've been able to put together with respect to documents and the evidence, the bulk of this unit was deployed on a battle front in the area or the zone of the Birac Infantry Brigade. There are some individuals who may be members of the 5th Military Police Battalion that touch around the actual area of Srebrenica or the crime scenes. But the bulk of the formation is not involved as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the 5th Communications Battalion.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, this unit, again by its design, is the unit that provides the communication backbone for the Drina Corps. When I say "backbone," it's the communication nodes, the radio relay sites for multichannel communication. That's their function. In this particular case they had deployed a mobile communications vehicle to the corps forward command post or IKM, in Pribicevac. And Major Milenko Jevtevic is there as part of that organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And the 4th Drinski Battalion or Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Okay. This particular unit, the 4th Drinski Brigade, is not a normal part of the organisation. Again, as a reflection of an overall shortage of manpower, what the VRS, and specifically the Drina Corps, on many occasions had to do was to essentially put together a composite formation in response to tasking by the Main Staff to provide a one or two battalion-sized formation for a particular part of the battlefield. In this particular case, the 4th Drinski Brigade was composed of elements of the Zvornik Brigade, elements of the Birac Brigade, some elements of the Bratunac Brigade, and were deployed on Trnovo on the Sarajevo battle front. Of course, one of the consequences to this is when we're looking at the period of 12 and 13 and 14 July, when the unit commanders are talking about having no manpower, it's because in most cases not only does the manpower completely stretched to the zones where they're in, but hundreds of their own zones are deployed out of sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, it's time for a break. Yes, we'll have 30 minutes break. We'll resume at 5 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, we've just finished off the overview for the Drina Corps. And so now I want to ask you about the Zvornik and Bratunac Brigades. We had seen a map of the zone of the Drina Corps. Did the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigade have a zone delineation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Within the zone of the Drina Corps, both of those units did have their own zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So we're now looking at P85. Can you tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: This particular document is a computer-generated map graphic that outlines the zones of responsibility of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade and the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you mean by zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: One of the hallmarks of the VRS, particularly on the basis of when it was organised or the way it was organised in 1992, was that the brigades were given broad but delineated areas of responsibility or zones of responsibility. In many cases they corresponded to rough municipal borders that were in existence or geographic zones. And the brigade was responsible for the conduct of military operations within this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this exhibit, did you assist in marking the zones of responsibility for this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the Bratunac Brigade, can you show us briefly where those zones are or that zone is, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: For the Bratunac Brigade, the general zone corresponds from roughly the Drina River towards Drinjaca, Konjevic Polje, down but just around Nova Kasaba, does not control Nova Kasaba. More or less a straight line towards a mountaintop down here and it's more accurate on the map, on this map here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to that map in a minute and give it an --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: And then around what covers in a large part what was then considered the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And on what material or information did you rely in drawing or assisting in drawing P85?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: With respect to the Zvornik Brigade zone, as part of the seizure of documents and material in the Zvornik Brigade, there were a number of maps which had a zone of operations delineated on it, the area of responsibility. The same applies with the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade and a number of documents that were seized from that location. This particular one which I believe is listed as Prosecution Exhibit P369, I believe. This was a map from the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, dated roughly 1992, early 1993, which delineates the Bratunac Brigade zone of responsibility. Now, further in this case what I was able to do is one of the documents we had seized was the war history of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. And as part of that war history, it defined the same brigade boundaries that correspond to the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So looking at 369, did you make any markings on this map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: There is one marking that is attributed to me on this map. If you will look on this sticker here, I was involved in part of the process for once the material came back from the field from the Bratunac Brigade, to catalogue this material and index it. And as a part of doing that, what we did was each and every document received an index number. And in this particular case that index number is listed as E15001 and my initials, RB. So I was the particular person who indexed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you do anything relating to the filled-in features that identify the zone of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir. Other than this sticker that I placed on it for accountability purposes, I didn't put any marks on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, let's talk briefly about the structure of the brigades that Mr. Jokic is from, the Zvornik Brigade, and the brigade that Mr. Blagojevic is from, the Bratunac Brigade. Let's start with the Zvornik Brigade and let's go with Exhibit P367, a line-and-block chart. Did you assist in developing this line-and-block chart?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And just -- you've described in very brief terms how the corps was formed in terms of the various organs and command structure. Can you do the same with the brigades and relate that to the structure of the corps.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, just the same as the VRS corps's structure is mirrored at the Main Staff level, at the brigade it tends to be as close as possible to that same mirror. For example, you will find in this brigade, this is the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, you will have a commander, you will have a chief of staff, you will have your operations and training organ, your intelligence organ, and your other associated organs and branches which are part of the brigade staff. You have an assistant commander or chief of moral, legal, and religious affairs for the brigade. You will have an assistant commander for security affairs, the security organ or the chief of the security organ as he's called. And you will have your rear services or logistics organ and an assistant commander for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And a corps has brigades attached to it. Does a brigade have fighting units attached to it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, in the brigade structure, the combat power or unit informations are devolved into the infantry battalions, or in some cases separate armour or infantry companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we get into this brigade in particular, I note this is called the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade. Can you compare that with the -- what we have known -- Bratunac to be called the 1st Light Infantry Brigade. What's the difference?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, structurally speaking, the difference is that a light infantry brigade, being more biased towards light infantry forces, will not have a lot of the staff elements that you would normally find in a normal brigade. For example, in a light infantry brigade, you will not have an armour officer or staff position, some of those types of things. One of the most significant differences, particularly with respect to the issue of Srebrenica 1995, is that in the light infantry brigade structure as designed, the role of security and intelligence is combined under one office; it's not broken into two offices. So in the Zvornik Brigade you will have an assistant commander for security affairs and a chief of intelligence. By doctrine or by their regulations for a light brigade structure, you will have in a light brigade, one assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about the Drina Corps? How did they break down intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: The Drina Corps structure resembles that of a regular brigade. You have a designated assistant commander for security affairs or a chief of security, and you will have a chief of intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about the Main Staff? How does the Main Staff break down in intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: In that particular instance, the Main Staff person in charge who in this case is General Tolimir, he is known as the assistant commander for intelligence and security. And his subordinate staff is broken into a security branch or a security department and an intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is similar to --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: It actually is more similar to the light infantry brigade as opposed to a regular infantry brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at the Zvornik Infantry Brigade structure. And I just want to -- you've already gone over the basic units, so I just want to focus you on the position of chief of engineering. Where does that fit into the structure? I don't want to get into the definition of that job right now, but how does it work in the -- how is it in the command structure?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Within the command structure, the chief of engineering is considered a member of the brigade staff, and he is subordinate to the chief of staff. So he's considered part of the brigade staff under the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we'll get into his relationship with the engineering company a little later. Can you just again quickly go to the security box in the Zvornik Brigade, and like you had done with others, tell us about any people in there that we may be seeing.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: With respect to the security organ, one of the key players is Lieutenant Drago Nikolic who is functioning as the assistant commander for security affairs of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. He is noted at the IKM of the Zvornik Brigade on the evening of 13 July. And as indicated by Colonel Obrenovic, at a point in time that evening, he is released from the IKM and he begins to become involved in the actual processing of Bosnian Muslim men who have come up from the Bratunac area and in their executions. And he is involved in executions at Orahovac and other locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I guess at this point I would like to register an objection to this gentleman testifying to what other witnesses have said in this particular case. Unless he is testifying from information that he had outside witness testimony, I would prefer that his answers include only what he is aware of from his personal observations as opposed to now testifying as if it were gospel what other witnesses have stated in this particular case. Because you are the finders of the fact. You have yet to make a determination whether the testimonies of Nikolic or Obrenovic or any other witnesses are true, accurate, and complete, and reliable in this instance. So given the answer that he has given, I understand he wishes to incorporate all this information, and also, as I understand the question that was posed, it was very limited in nature and properly so. So just to -- so we have a clear record as to what he actually knows. And now he's being asked to describe a position as opposed to what an individual did according to what another witness has testified in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think the witness gave us a very good answer. During his answer he might cite whatever the other person said in this particular case. We did not give any findings at this moment, and this is not the subject of the present proceedings. But later on, I believe that we will come into the very details of these incidents. Let us allow Mr. McCloskey to proceed while remembering that there is an objection in this aspect from the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And just in a brief response, I am -- do not intend to ask Mr. Butler to carefully go through the testimony of critical people and evaluate it. I do agree that that is for the Court. This is merely for some background, and he, of course, may mention what various people have testified to, if it's important and relevant to some document or some other exhibit. But I did not intend to have him -- or question him at length about what other people have said. We want to get Mr. Butler home for Thanksgiving and we would be here a long time if we did that. So we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So that's for Mr. Nikolic. How about a brief -- where might we see or hear from the other person in that security organ? Who is that and what is his position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: That individual is an individual Captain Milorad Trbic. He is considered to be a security officer. He is an individual who shows up with respect to the intercepts on 16 and 17 July. He's also functioning on 16th and 17th July as the duty officer of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to the -- talk about the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade structure. If we could look at P368. Again you have described the -- roughly the structure of a light infantry brigade. But before we -- well, let's go briefly into the structure. We see the commander in July is, of course, the accused, Vidoje Blagojevic. The chief of staff, deputy commander, what can you tell us about this person.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: In July of 1995, that individual is Major Radomir Pantic [phoen]. He is the chief of staff and deputy commander. The issue with him is on 13 July 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you just check that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Novica Pajic. My apologies. It doesn't show up well on the screen here. He is the chief of staff, deputy commander in July of 1995. On 13 July 1995, he is assigned to lead an 80-person combat group in the zone of the Milici Brigade. So we don't have a lot of information concerning him, other than on the afternoon of 13 July he is assigned to lead a combat group out of the zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let me ask you about -- let's go to the security and intelligence organ. I won't ask you about Mr. Nikolic. We've had a lot on Mr. Nikolic. How about Captain First Class Dragisa Jovanovic. Who's he? What can you tell us where he might show up in this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: He's an individual who, as I've recently learned, was appointed the intelligence officer of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. So notwithstanding the JNA structure, there was apparently a decision to split the intelligence and security functions. In this particular instance, that officer during the period in question, we have documents and orders which indicate that he was accompanying Bratunac Brigade soldiers who were deployed to the Trnovo battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what about in the rear services, what can you tell us about Major Trisic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Major Trisic is the assistant commander for rear services for the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. From the available information that I have, he was present in and around the Bratunac headquarters during the period. And there will be select references to him on the basis of documents or some of the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we go into some of your highlights regarding the roles and responsibilities of a commander, can you describe to us briefly, in July 1995 how well equipped and organised was the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: With respect to organisation, they were organised like any of the other light infantry brigades within the Drina Corps. With respect to equipment, personnel, manning, things of that nature, comparable to modern military forces, they would not compare very favourably at all. Like all of the other units in the VRS, they were undermanned, they were understaffed. In the particular case of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, there were a very few, very limited number of officers who were actually officers from the former JNA who had active service and were professional officers. With the exception of the accused and his chief of staff, those were the only -- they were the only two people. All of the other officers were reserve officers. All of the junior officers in the battalions, most of the non-commissioned officers filling those positions were reservists who were mobilised in 1992 and were fighting the war as reservists. With respect to manning, the Bratunac Brigade like all of the other brigades always was short of troops and they suffered a problem with troops deserting their positions and not returning after leave or not returning after a two-week break from the lines. So with respect for that particular brigade, it was a significant issue. However, the brigade with respect to other VRS units in the Drina Corps, particularly light infantry brigades, was no better or no worse off. So that was the standard at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's now go into some of the high points or the key points in the -- defining the concept of superior command, a commander's responsibility. Was this a subject of your command report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: One of the key topics of my command report was identifying the mechanism of command and the mechanisms by which a commander exercises command over subordinates within the VRS. In this respect, the documents and the regulations of the former JNA with respect to the brigade rules are extremely enlightening on that. At the same time, the documents pertaining to JNA command staff operations and procedures also lay out those mechanisms and the interfaces that occur within the military structure. And again as part of my analysis, looking to see if those models applied to the JNA and the VRS and particularly to the Bratunac and Zvornik Infantry Brigades, they, in fact, do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you identified some of those rules and regulations for this -- for your discussion on this topic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the first one that we have is P370/A. And can you tell us, Mr. Butler, just briefly what this document is and then direct us to the key points relating to the command issue that you wanted to point out.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: This document is, of course, the English translation of the brigade rules for infantry, motorised, mountain, alpine, marine and light infantry brigades of the former SFRY. It is dated 1984. However, in conducting my analysis, it is clear that these regulations remained in effect during the constituent period and were the basic operating framework by which VRS brigades functioned in 1985. With respect to brigade command, paragraph 115 essentially lays that out. It indicates that the brigade commander has the exclusive right to command all brigade units and attached units. And that he bears full responsibility for the work of the brigade command and subordinate commands for the state of morale, for security, and combat readiness for training, and for the proper performance of tasks. That in effect it encompasses a principle broadly known not only within the SFRY military doctrine, but in almost all military doctrines universally as unity of command, that is, the commander, he is the single individual with right of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can the commander delegate his responsibility to others?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: As a general function of the command and staff process, a commander can and does delegate responsibility for the conduct of tasks to his subordinates. That delegation can be codified in regulations such as the delegated responsibilities of officers on his staff by position, be it an operations officer, an air defence officer, an engineer officer, a rear services or security, or it could be a non-codified one which is when an individual is a duty officer. But one of the things it comes back to is while the commander can delegate the authority for the accomplishment of a mission, that ultimately the commander retains the responsibility for the accomplishment of that task or mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And the last sentence in the first paragraph: "The commander takes decisions, assigns tasks to units, monitors their fulfillment, and demands their strict execution regardless of the difficulties that arise." In simple terms, can you tell us what that amounts to on the ground.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: That is essentially the function of command. Taking the decisions, assigning tasks, delegating the authority to conduct those tasks. One of the key things of command is monitoring their fulfillment. Within the concept of JNA command, it's not enough for a commander to give an order and leave it. That commander is -- and part why his staff exists is to ensure that once that order is given it is carried out in full and that the compliance of that order is reported back. So it's not just enough to give an order and assume it's been completed. A commander is required under these regulations and as part of his command to verify compliance with those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. The next paragraph: "Through his personal conduct, work involvement in the implementation of the SKJ policies, ethical standing, courage, ability, fairness, cool-headedness," and it goes on. "The commander vitally influences the entire condition of the brigade, especially the morale of his units and command." What does that really amount to in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: The commander is, in effect, he is the linchpin by which the brigade operates around. I believe perhaps the best way to put it would be to quote General Dannatt who testified several years back here where he indicated that command is a personal thing. The -- no other person within the brigade has more influence on how the brigade functions or does not function as the commander. It is his to command. And as you can see in this document, the issue of command is not just a series of professional schools or qualities or check blocks. Many of these issues of command are personal character traits: Ethical standing, courage, ability, fairness. I mean, these are all characteristics and qualities of command. And I would say not only in the SFRY or former JNA or VRS, but these are standard throughout most military units. These are what people look for in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document that you've chosen to help us understand command, P374. First of all, this says -- well, P374 is the -- it should be the military lexicon definition.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Sorry. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us, this is a quote from the 1981 JNA military lexicon. What is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: A military lexicon is essentially the military version of a dictionary which gives the definitions of many of the arcane or complex terms that the military tends to use. It's generally an important document within all militaries, because it is essential from a military standpoint that everyone recognises and understands intrinsically what basic principles are, how they're defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've heard in this court already the principle of unity of command. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: In essence, unity of command is the general military philosophy that only one individual can be in command of one unit -- or of one series of units. You cannot have a function where you have multiple commanders in one unit. I think historically that approach has been found to not work effectively on the battlefield, and I'm not aware of any armed forces that conducts military operations where they have a dual or three- or four-part command. It is command centralised on the individual, the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to the next document that you have that helps us identify key command principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have 371? Can you tell us first of all what -- this is entitled "Provisional service regulations of the Army of the Serbian Republic." What is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war or beginning of the conflict in Bosnia starting from roughly May onwards, the entity that later became known as the Republika Srpska went by the name of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So what this document is are the service regulations for that army, the Army of Serbian Republic of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And directing your attention to what should be page 10, relations in the army, "Giving Orders". Paragraph 17. "Members of the army shall carry out the orders of their superiors without demur, in full, accurately, and punctually. If by any chance the order was not given in good time, the person is required to take measures and act in accordance with the specific situation." Now, what is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, the service regulations are the regulations that are bound to -- by every service member in the VRS. This particular paragraph essentially categorises the fact that an army, and the VRS is an army, operates on a system where orders have to be complied with, fully and without demur.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's not unique to this army, I take it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: That is a basic function in every military that I know of, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next exhibit you've chosen, 372/A, page 15. And it -- starting at paragraph 13, 14, 15, 16, 17 --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: If it's possible to scroll the ELMO down a little bit, we can... Or scroll up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why have you chosen these paragraphs? Can you explain in simple terms their importance in command.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: First if I may, this document is referred to as what we call the command and staff rules. It's the work of the command and staff. And what this document does is in great detail explain how command and staff process works on an organised military staff. And of course that would include a brigade. When a lot of the terms that come out that you will see in military orders, sometimes these terms have a different meaning in both a western connotation, or even in a military connotation. And what does document does is in effect list out what some of these terms are and what is meant by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So 13.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Essentially lays out what the term "command" is. A process or function of control. The content is the assignment of tasks by command documents, which orders, commands, orders, directives and instructions. A command act communicates a commander's decision and activates the process of the task's execution. Moving to paragraph 14, the phrase "coordination," in this military sense, is a function of command and control, in ensuring that the various elements in the execution of the task have been set. Moving down to paragraph 15: Issue of cooperation is also a form of coordination which harmonises the combat operations carried out by units. One of the important things to note here, with the phrase of cooperation is that cooperation is organised by commanding officers in the staffs normally at all levels of command and control. However, if we go to the next page, it notes that it's -- the terms of cooperation or cooperation orders are pursuant to the decisions of the commanding officer. So it's the commander who defines the terms of cooperation and organisations it for the subordinates to, in effect, do that cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do we see this term actually used in some documents that you'll be discussing later on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: We will see the term "cooperation" in a number of the documents particularly relevant between the relationship between army units on the ground in or near Bratunac and Zvornik, and RS MUP units that are operating in that same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then what about collaboration, number 16.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, collaboration, as it says, is a manner of regulating the relations between unit commands and control organs of other non-military types of units. Again, in this sense it's dedicated to the function and support of combat tasks in the combat area. Collaboration achieves a consensus on the manner of which armed combat is to be unified and ensures the integrity or materialisation or the fulfillment of the commander's decisions. In this case, the basis for collaboration is provided by the superior command. The phrase collaboration does not necessarily, and I think in this one it spells out fairly clearly, does not imply a command relationship. A collaboration is more of a relationship that in a western parlance we would see as cooperative. That's why it's important to get the terminology correct in the way the JNA uses it. In many things when we look at the phrase cooperation, from a western military standpoint, that's not a term that implies a command relationship. However, within the doctrine of the former JNA, that term does imply a command relationship. And the other term that doesn't is collaboration. So that's why the specificity of the terms is important in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And lastly, verification. Verification is a process function of command and control. Does that fit into any of the other definitions you've talked about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: Again, wrapping back to the issue of the overall function of command, verification is, again, that process of a commander or a giver of orders ensuring that the orders have been complied with. That is a function of command and at the higher levels, brigade staff and above being part of those higher levels, in many cases that verification is a function of the brigade staff and why it exists to support the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, have you -- can you give us any sort of practical examples of documents that show how command works, in particular in the Zvornik and Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: As part of my analysis into whether or not these JNA rules and regulations were applicable to the VRS several years down the line, one of the things we did when looking through the documents and doing research is to find documents, orders, or directives, which would affect these JNA rules and regulations. This particular document is Prosecution Exhibit 376. This is a document which was from the Zvornik, at that time, Light Infantry Brigade, which is the delineation of the duties and tasks of the command staff and staff organs. As you can see in the opening paragraph, it is directly based on the rules of the brigade and the relevant paragraphs. So in this sense, it's a validation that the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, or Light Infantry Brigade as it was back then, is adopting and is following as part of their regulatory basis those rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you have any indication that the Bratunac Brigade was doing the same thing, following those basic rules?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: This is a document which was obtained by the OTP in its search of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is Exhibit 377/A.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER
utterances.text: And again it is a document which defines the command and staff process. Now, unlike the document from the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade, this one does not have the commander's signature and it does not have any indication or something which I can date it by, per se. However, my analysis of this indicates that again it is a direct lift from the JNA 1984 brigade regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's probably a good time to break. We go into another area after this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have to break now. Witness, I have to remind you, as I did to other witnesses, that while you are in The Hague, you are under the oath. So do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've spoken briefly to Mr. Karnavas. I haven't had a chance to speak to Mr. Stojanovic, but we of course will abide by that normal rule. However, in terms of an expert that may be testifying for a while, sometimes there's logistical items where we may need to talk about; when he's coming and what exhibits might be next. To that degree if there's no disagreement, if all of us could deal on those practical logistical ways with our experts, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I hope somebody from the registrar could also be present at your meeting with this witness if it's only concerning logistical matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I'll talk to the registry about that. Your Honour, also just one other complication is, as you're aware, the Krstic appeal hearing is scheduled in November. And Mr. Butler has -- does sometimes provide assistance and help to the appellate staff or other people involved. Now, that may cover the subjects of his testimony, because of course it's the same subject, but it has nothing to do with his testimony. But I did want people to be aware of that. If there are any concerns or problems -- he's not real active in that appeal, but sometimes it's helpful for the appellate attorneys to ask Mr. Butler about a document or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I don't know what to say about the appeal process. I'm unaware of why -- the reasons why an appellate lawyer would need to consult with a witness, unless it's a Rule 115, as we have here, as it applies in this Tribunal. But as far as the appeals process is based on the record, it's based on the facts that are in the record, it's based on the law. So unless the gentleman is going to be providing testimony, I see no reason. Having said that, knowing the individuals that are working on the appeal, I have no problem, you know, assuming that there are some strict guidelines, like they separate Krstic versus this particular case. And I understand the difficulties. As far as the first request is concerned, as I indicated to Mr. McCloskey, I'm very flexible in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Mr. Stojanovic, are you in a position to give a reply for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as for our Defence, although I did not talk to Mr. McCloskey during the break because I was speaking to my client, we believe -- our Defence believes that generally speaking there will be no problem with this. Organisationally, logistically, in order to have this expert heard, it can be done. Now, it is for you to say whether it's going to be in the presence of someone from the registry or not. But we certainly leave that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Mr. McCloskey, I think your request is granted by this Bench. And I hope there could be somebody very neutral in this case to be present during that talk. And I believe that you will discuss it with our Court Deputy. So we'll resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning in the same courtroom.
